review:
[b]Wow, I wished I had picked up [i]Northgard[/i] sooner.[/b] This is very much a modernized version of [i]Age of Empires[/i] with some boardgame-like elements. Normally, I hate elements that are boardgame-like, but it works [i]really[/i] well here. Also, I gotta say that you wouldn't even know this was Early Access with how polished and full of content it is (I did have one crash, though). I booted it up and four hours flew by. Took me about an hour to get my head around the mechanics. 

[i]Essentially, this is a RTS game with a variety of victory conditions.[/i] Everything is fully customizable. I only played single player and that mode is great; I'm excited to try multiplayer. Because it has multiplayer, there is no manipulation of time or pausing. Some refer to this title as a 'city builder', but I don't see really any aspects of city building - it's a RTS like [i]Age of Empires[/i]. [b]What really makes [i]Northgard[/i] stand out from the pack is how the map is built from large tiles.[/b] The tiles create a whole new dimension to how you go about playing the game. Here are some interesting things:
[list]
[*] You can only build on your tiles, and each tile has a colonization cost (usually food).
[*] Not all tiles are created equal; many have powerful resources and/or buffs associated with them.
[*] There is a special victory condition associated with a tile on each map; there are variations of this tile that are quite unique. For example, one I had to colonize was covered in magma. Once I got there, I needed to build a forge and then craft a special sword. Once I crafted it, I won. It was neat.
[/list]
[b]Everything felt great, overall.[/b] I'll definitely be dumping time into this one. I like the achievements, too.

[b]Pros:[/b]
+Very polished and full of content already
+While staying true to the RTS genre, it definitely brings tons of fresh new ideas and mechanics to the table; the tiles are an outstanding addition
+UI is super clean and easy to understand
+Music and artwork are great
+The currently available factions all have cool attributes and lend themselves well to varying strategy

[b]Cons:[/b]
-Honestly, I haven't found anything to really nit-pick about yet

[b]If you liked [i]Age of Empires[/i], ya gotta give this a go.[/b] It's worth it even at full price.

The Theme is cool, vikings, good voice acting, and the in-game world is lovely.
The concept is great, you can achieve victory by various means.  
You can battle to win, study lore to win, create artifacts to win, or become so popular that you win.  

Well, there is one really bad part of this game that spoils all the enjoyment.

The Artificial  Intelligence (AI) is terrible.  I mean, really, terribly awful.

The enemy will always be some % of your progress, depending on the difficulty you choose.
So on easy, you are ahead of the enemy. They will attack you once every year or two.
On medium, the enemies are usually ahead of you in most ways. They will attack a couple times a year.
On hard, the enemies are always ahead of you and attack your borders 4 times per in-game year.
On extreme, they are always ahead of you, and constantly attack your borders.

Sounds ok, if the enemy actually suffered any loss.
Nope!

The AI has infinite, unlimited, instant resources.
It automatically spawns a new hero, automatically generates a new military force, and suffers no resource costs.

If there is more than 1 AI enemy on a map, they ALL attack you and ONLY you.  They never fight each other. They might fight Draugr and Wolves.. but that is just to expand the AI territory.

Basically, the AI makes this game so linear, so basic, so simple, that it absolutely loses all flavor.

You cannot explore because you must hurry and satisfy the win-con versus the AI.

You cannot enjoy a city-builder, because you must build the following buildings; x-y-z in that order, so the AI doesn't ROFLstomp you.

There is a single procedure to win.  
1) Scouts and Lumber, build houses
2) Expand territory and harvest Food & Stone until you hit an enemy border.
3) Military, Forge, and City Hall upgrade, so you can make your warchief.
4) Trade, Iron, and Fortifications so you can unlock upgrades.
5) Defend zone-by-zone against enemy raiders
6) Rebuild any zones you lose.
7) Wait approximately 1 hour for win conditions to be satisfied (unless conquest, then you mass up troops and go straight for the enemy city hall, skip any skirmishes and border fights, just hit their main base, done.  Rinse, repeat for each enemy).


Sure, you can sometimes choose that process, based on the map.

Maybe you spawn near lots of food and iron, so you can go for military might.
Maybe you spawn near a bunch of lore stones, and shoreline so you can do that.
Maybe you spawn near lots of stone and monsters so you can go for fame wins.

Point is, you really just have a couple minutes to survey your map, make a decision on which of the win-cons you will focus on, then spam spam spam the same boring routine until iWin.

There is nothing original about it, the clans have different stats that make some victories more tangible.
So if playing hard or extreme, your choice of clan matters.  In normal and easy, the choice of clan can be a stabilizing factor for a more chillax experience.

But, ultimately, you are still just racing against time to obtain win-con.

I don't like 'timed-event' games like this. If I want to take my time doing things, that should be possible, but not in Northgard.  You are just being rushed and harried through a messy gameplay to a basic win-con that leaves you feeling flustered, and disinterested.  Like, why did I just spend an hour for this?

Graphically cute, the concept advertised is not what this game is.  It is not a city builder.  It is not a sim.  It is not RPG.  It is not adventure.  Once you figure out the process, the win-pocedures, the game is the same experience EVERY time.  You just go thru the steps, 1-2-3 win. 1-2-3 win.  Unless the AI just randomly decides to win.  It can do that, because unlimited resource pool, instant spawns, and spontaneous progress.  

Bottom line: the AI sucks, and the game is boring because of it.  Really boring. The developers really need to change the AI to behave within limits of resources, time, and progress.  But instead, the devs are just creating new variations on the theme..
Buy new clan!  Spend microtransaction on bad game!  No thanks.  I bought it on sale, and I regret the purchase.  It is not worth $11.  I would consider this game to still be under development, and should be Free-to-Play if they are going to also sell so much additional content. 

I guess the campaign is worth paying through once.  That's kinda neat.  I really did like the voice acting.

After 1,300+ hours, I finally completed all the achievements in this game! 🎉
I’d like to share my experience with you:

Story Mode:
Rig’s Saga – A fantastic introduction to the game. A must-play for beginners.
Cross of Vidar – A challenging story mode. Not recommended for inexperienced players.
Overall – Both storylines have solid lore and satisfying endings.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

Conquest Mode (a.k.a. The Grind Zone):
This is where 90% of the grind happens—50 wins with each clan! Here’s my take on them:

Favorite Clan: Horse 🐎
Why? Two heroes that cost no iron, can be upgraded multiple times, and even craft their own gear.
Bonus: No need to waste villagers on blacksmithing.
Result: Max upgrades within 3 years + Altar of Kings.

Easiest Clan: Stag 🦌
Why? Starts with extra resources, and Skalds generate both Happiness and Gold.
Verdict: Easily the most beginner-friendly clan.

Hardest Clan: Hounds 🐺
Why? I just couldn’t figure them out. Even with upgraded brawlers and a mixed army, I kept getting wrecked.
Verdict: If someone has tips, I’m all ears!

Weakest Clan: Goat 🐐
Why? I think we all know why…

Most Boring Clan: Rat 🐀
Why? Mid-game becomes a chore. Managing shamans on every tile for healing, then scrambling to reposition them during enemy attacks—over and over again.
Bonus Frustration: AI armies magically respawn like they have infinite gold, leading to 3-4 full-strength invasions per year.
Result: I often saved and quit out of pure exhaustion.

Most Overpowered Clan: Turtle 🐢
Why? Caravans gather resources without buildings.
Double harvesting from farms, fishing, and hunting.
Villagers can be bought with food, making population growth effortless.
Gold production is a higher —100+ food production within 5 years is easy.
Verdict: I wouldn’t be surprised if they get nerfed soon.

Most Unique/Weird Clan: Owl 🦉
Why? No wood, buildings are constructed with Lore, completely unique tech tree, and a “boss” unit.
Verdict: Very different playstyle, takes some getting used to.

The Other Clans:
Pretty well-balanced overall, each with its pros and cons.

-----------------------------------------------------------------

Bifrost Mode:
First attempts? Brutal. Even on the easiest difficulty, it felt nearly impossible.
After multiple tries? You start understanding the mechanics and making better choices.
Verdict: Tough learning curve, but once mastered, it’s extremely satisfying to win.

-----------------------------------------------------------------

Multiplayer Experience:
Why I didn’t play MP much: 90% of games are just Snake Clan rushing in 801.
Biggest issue: Finding matches where people actually develop their clans instead of speed-running aggression is rare.
Verdict: I’d rather play other RTS games for a more strategic multiplayer experience.
---------------------------------------------------------------

Final Thoughts:

If you made it this far, thanks for reading! 😊
Hope you enjoy this game as much as I did! =D

PRO

The game clock runs through the seasons, and you need more wood and food during the Winter, so plan accordingly.  Most of your regular citizen jobs are "set-it-and-forget-it" types.  For example, assign a citizen to chop wood, and as long as things are going good you'll never have to mess with that citizen again.  Just check on your "job slots" now and then to make sure they are still filled.

CON
I wish I hadn't spent so much money buying all of the DLC clans.  Game play doesn't seem to be that much different when using another clan.  For many players, just playing the base game would be satisfactory enough without the extra clans.

As a novice to RTS games and a poor min/maxer, Northgard is the first RTS I have not rage quit. Not only that, I love it.

Pros:
- Games generally last between 1.5-2 hours, so you can actually finish it before the heat death of the universe.
- Looks beautiful! Both stylized and well-executed environments and characters make Northgard shine.
- Distilled essence of RTS means a low entry barrier.
- Never too much clutter on screen.
- While the campaign [strike]plot[/strike] tutorial isn't memorable, it is a good intro to each clan.
- I did not have to read a 200-page Steam guide to win.
- No problems with unranked/invited friends for multiplayer.

Cons:
- The game is simple for an RTS. What makes matches shorter and the game less intimidating also make for less mastery satisfaction. If you are an RTS veteran, or enjoy more complex TBS like Civ, Northgard may not be for you.
- Not all clans are created equal. Particularly some of the DLC clans (Lynx and Dragon, I'm looking at you) are handicapped.
- Explicitly the Dragon's thralls could use more indication as to what they're assigned to.
- It'd be nice to preview each clan's information while in the mutiplayer lobby.

I have about 800 hours in this game, it's my weekend co-op with my wife. We're fairly casual gamers that enjoy a slow paced game. We've both been pretty unhappy with the roadmap of the game over the last year or so. A lot of what makes the clans fun has been removed or nerfed. Every time a clan DLC is released the game is just riddled with glitches in multiplayer. 

In this most recent patch, I've noticed the following: towers are basically worthless, raven raiding ships now move at light speed giving you almost no time to react, my most recent game I was at negative (or close to) food for the first half of the game despite half of my squares being food squares while playing the newest clan, which ground expansion to a halt. I've hardly ever had issues with food production in the game in the past. Playing against Raven was intense, they were blitzing me every few months and the AI was set on easy mode. Strangely when I finally managed to muster the army to fend them off, they just quit attacking me. 

Over the years there also were a lot of fun mechanics that took a huge hit, like Kraken. I would've much preferred that the devs lift up the other weaker clans instead of nerfing the few fun ones. Only a few clans have scaling in late game play. I was excited for the newest clan because they were advertised as a clan that was ideal for a player like me, but they just wind up taking a beating when facing other clans.

If I had to guess, I'd say the devs are balancing the game for really small maps of extremely skilled players that play Domination only. That's fine for the top 5-10% of players but really sucks out the fun for the casual players. I wish we could go back to a few years ago when the game was a lot more fun.

Despite being an RTS, Northgard plays more like a Civ game, in which your primary focus is maintaining balance between happiness, food, wood, lore (science), krowns (money), and military power. Since each map is randomly generated, you'll find that your approach to victory depends not only on your chosen faction but also the resources available near your starting position. This map generation is what keeps this game replayable and repeatable.

However I must admit that combat can be repetitive, since at the moment there are only three types of fighting units. Some factions have unique warchiefs (general unit) but their attack power is more or less the same. Their uniqueness affects resource management instead.

CONS
- Right now, there are no hotkeys yet for units, which make defending and microing against attacks a chore.
- Repetitive combat, needs more unit types, with more unique mechanics.
- Needs customizable victory conditions. Whenever you start a game, you can tick boxes if you want a fame victory, trade victory, domination victory, etc. But the magnitude of these victory conditions are fixed. For example, fame victory requires 1200 fame---I wish there was a slider that allows me to change this to mayble 1400 or 1000 fame. I really think these victory sliders would allow players to decide how long each game lasts, since each game lasts roughly about an hour.

PROS
+Randomly generated maps, map objectives and map events make each playthrough challenging and unique.
+System requirements are quite low. The game can run on low end PC's and laptops
+Decent comeback mechanics. Being beaten in a fight does not mean you lose the game.
+Easy to learn, hard to master. 

DEPENDS ON TASTE
+/- Economy management requires IQ. Not only do you have to sustain your town's needs in a summer/winter cycle, you also have to prepare for game events. Thankfully these events have early warnings (usually several months ahead of such catastrophe) so if you mess up, it's probably your own fault for mismanaging your resources. I like this challenge, though I know of others who hate it.

I recommend this game, especially if you like Civ and would like to play a more casual, RTS version of it.

I like the "simple to learn, hard to master" style this game gives you. You're tasked to manage three basic resources, securing sections of the map to further develop those resources and other mid- and late-game ones. I have never played PvP so I cannot speak to that, but I do like the conquest (both solo and with a partner) and playing with/against the AI. 

The one thing that I really dislike is the fact that each additional clan is $5. Sure, you don't have to get them, but the base game without it almost feels incomplete. The clans are built to expand upon the game and offer new features that are meant to appeal to the players. I mean, I guess that's why they slapped a $5 price tag on em, and why I've bought all of them. But, I feel like it's the same as having to pay to play Trevor or Franklin in GTA V, or paying to access tools beyond copper level in Stardew Valley. You may not need to to play the game, but it'll either be tedious, repetitive, or simply incomplete. I'm not saying give out the DLC clans for free, I understand that folks at Shiro Games need to eat and pay bills, but I hope they would consider an alternative way to acquire the DLC clans. Maybe through in game currency, or with a season pass or bundle deal. Or possibly with a trial version for the clan (i.e. one single player game, or 20 minutes of gameplay, etc) so folks can test it out and see if it fits their play style. There are a couple of clans that I probably would have passed on if I got a chance to try them first, simply because they don't fit my play style, not 'cause they're poorly made or something.

Bought it on a whim and ended up enjoying it quite a bit. Whether you are new to RTS type games, or a veteran, I think this would be a great game for your library. The dynamics of having to maintain the different resources, especially once winter hits, is well done and it feels like you are accomplishing something. With a variety of ways to win the game, really the choice is up to you on how you want to eek out your victory.

Pros: Design and look of the game. The game play itself, you can tell the game developers spent a lot of time and love on this game. The controls are familiar. The variety of game play styles makes it worth playing it again and again.

Cons: Not much really. In game tutorial isn't as in depth as it could be. As someone who plays a LOT of RTS style games, it still had a bit of a learning curve (which was easily overcame via youtube videos). I don't like that I have to pay more for the additional clans, though I will for this game, kinda wish it was just part of the game itself. Sadly, I'm aware, this is kinda the norm anymore. /sigh I miss the "one and done" features of older games lol

I'm a nobody, an unknown (I know this), but for those of you who bother to read this. I give this game a solid 8 out of 10. Worth buying, and if you find it on sale, bundled with the additional clans, definitely get it.

I have over 900 hours in Northgard, so this isn't a review from someone who just lost a few matches. I've played this game for years because I genuinely enjoyed it, but the current state of the game is incredibly disappointing.

The clan balance is a complete mess. Instead of properly balancing existing clans, it feels like every new DLC clan is released overtuned just to drive sales. Then it takes forever to address the obvious issues, if they get addressed at all.

On top of that, my recent multiplayer games have been filled with cheaters. Whether it's map hacks or other exploits, it's becoming more and more common, and it feels like there is little to no moderation.

The biggest problem is that it honestly seems like none of the developers actually play their own game at a high level. Many balance changes make no sense from a competitive perspective, and obvious issues remain untouched for months.

It's frustrating because Northgard has an amazing foundation, but right now it feels like it's being managed without understanding what makes the game enjoyable or fair.

I can't recommend it in its current state.

The developers seem to have gotten better about not breaking the game completely, but I'm still going to have to leave this as negative for now. In some ways the game solves the micromanagement problems found in other RTS games, in other ways it creates some micromanagement problems, but on the balance overall the micromanagement issues that you get with other 4X style RTS games are mostly avoided here. There is a little bit of a learning curve as a result of the uniqueness of the gameplay mechanics, but it's pretty easy to get over and the campaign does a good job of introducing you to the mechanics.  

Combat is simple, even though each clan has their own flavor. Don't expect complex strategy here... once you've played a few games it can become a simple matter of balancing your growth with your military capabilities, but there's also some flavor strategy between the clans that comes into play when thinking about your strategy.

These are pretty minor things, though. It's not like RTS strategy has ever been complex for any other title, and if what you've been looking for is a relaxing game that you can play to destress but still be actively engaged, this is a very rewarding purchase. What it aims to do it does well and does with style and consistency. 

 + Excellent music.
 + Very good and scalable performance, even in endgame.
 + Interesting and dynamic build decisions that reflect tile bonuses.
 + Unique clan playstyles, for the most part.
 + Unique mechanics and a seasonal planning consideration factor.

 - A bit repetitive, mostly simple mechanics with some artificial gating.

Overall, it's a fun game with a solid design that has the same weaknesses as many other RTS/4X style games. I recommend it and look forward to what the developer will do in the future.

So, lets talk about Norse Mythology: This game is filled with all things Odin, Ragnarak, and even the Kraken. Fans will find themselves filled to the brim with interesting Norse tales and trinkets scattered throughout the lands.

If you love strategy games such as Sid Meier's Civilization, Age of Wonders, and Endless Legend. You should give this one a chance. While those three are considered turn based tactics-Northgard takes a different approach to a well loved formula with Real time strategy. 

I've played about 50 solid hours, I beat the story mode, played on conquest and even did a little bit of local multiplayer with the husband. To say I love the game, is an understatement. Conquest is by far my favorite one of the bunch. It's a challenge that my husband and I can play/work together and while it's tough and thins our relationship sometimes-it's very, very fun and rewarding when we do move forward to the next challenge. I wish all strategy games had something as fun as this.

Other than the game play, the game is beautiful. Each clan has its own bit of flair to them and you really do end up picking favorites. Or, if you're like me, go headstrong into the wolfclan because you can't get past the darn story on hard mode. Wolfclan makes me cry. But after twenty games I think the aggression has leaked into my other strategy games. Even when I play another clan I still find myself racing to kill wolves and bears for no reason. As great as story mode is, single player is not why I love this game.

Also, last note: play the story mode! Please. I did it for the achievements, but I absolutely fell in love with each of the clan's main characters. (also bonus points for learning each one) There was this kind of magic that breathed life into it. The artwork between games was stunning, and the voice acting was wonderful. You can tell they put at lot of heart into it and for someone who loves a good story, I really appreciate that.

[h1][i]This is a review for the story/singleplayer mode of the game since I have not touched the multiplayer part, yet. The review is spoiler-free.[/i][/h1]

[h1]The gist of it:[/h1]
Northgard is quite an unexpectedly decent real-time strategy game, within the Norse universe, with its main focus being resource management, territory control and simplistic combat scenarios that will provide quite a challenge. 

👍 [u]The good parts:[/u]
+While the gameplay is the main focus, the story holds on its own as well even for an indie title.
+Very easy to get into the game's mechanics but hard to master on higher difficulties and possibly in multiplayer.
+Huge, colorful and well-detailed maps.
+Good soundtrack.
+Multiple clans to choose from that alter the gameplay a bit.

👎[u]The bad parts:[/u]
-No voice acting for the story characters.
-Simplistic in nature and may get repetitive or boring at times. 
-The story mode is unbalanced; AI basically cheats in higher difficulties; some clans are simply way better than the others.
-Performance issues even on a high-end PC.

[h1]The story[/h1]
The story, simply put, follows a quest for revenge for our main protagonist in which he'll have to ally with different clans commanded by interesting and unique characters which you'll be able to play as. Things will get complicated as you progress through the story and you learn more about why you were put in that situation. It's short and lasts about 14 hours or more depending on which difficulty you're playing. It's also worth mentioning that this seems like only the start of a major campaign either for future expansions or sequels. 

While the story isn't the most shocking and impressive thing out there, it will keep you going through its average length. Hopefully, we'll get more of its interesting Norse universe in the future. It would be a shame to leave us hanging as it did. 

Story score: 7/10

[h1]The gameplay[/h1]
Northgard is an RTS with its main focus being resource management/gathering and territory control. You can choose to play with different clans, each with its own unique ability and progression method. Some favor combat and fast-paced zone control, others favor a slower paced method like boosting the resources, as well as having unique skills or specifically lore skills which is another in-game resource that you can gather beside the usual ones we're used to like the coins, food, wood, etc. Lore skills are basically game advantages and are probably the most important aspect of all the resources since they can change the tide of a game easily.

The food resource comes with its different methods of gathering depending on the clan you play, either by fishing or by hunting or simply just killing all the animals in the games. Food is also very important because its required to capture a zone and the more you capture the more is needed. There is a clan however that can capture zones with coins. The other resources are used to mostly buy and upgrade your buildings as well as hiring mercenaries or building your small army. 

There's also a happiness meter in which you will have to maintain it at all times positive if you wish to keep receiving villagers that are used to help gather the specified resources. Each building and villager consumes wood, food, and coin to maintain so the more you grow the more it's needed to keep up with the necessities as well as the need to keep them happy(they can starve and die for example).

Now all this sounds simple enough however the game comes with a winter mechanic in which every year you'll have to survive the winter season, where resources drain a lot faster. This is where the lore resource comes in where it can hugely help in preventing the draining. It's a game changer and can easily turn a losing game into a winning one or vice-versa if you pick poorly. 

Combat is pretty much basic, there are 3 types of warrior, melee, shield and ranged as well as having your own special hero depending on the clan you selected. Each hero has a fame meter which grows by doing things in the game, like killing mythical creatures or capturing zones or completing objectives. Fame has 2 levels and each provides unique benefits. You won't have huge battles like in Total Rome and a bit less than Warcraft 3 but still decent enough to provide some fun and tactical advantages. 

Gameplay score: 8/10

[h1]Audio[/h1]
Not much can be said here, the soundtrack is pretty good overall and fits well with the atmosphere and the sound effects are as basic as they can be with nothing worthy of mentioning. Sadly regarding the story, there is no voice acting between the characters nor any banter between them in each chapter. It's all text. The story while small would've benefited A LOT if it had some good voice actors doing the characters. There's only the narrator or the main character voice that talks between chapters and he does a good job at it but not enough, for me personally at least. 

Audio score: 7.5/10

[h1]The graphics and tech analysis[/h1]
The game is pretty colorful and cartoonish, and it's nice to look at even if it does not offer high-end graphics. Zones are decent looking and quite unique from each other though they will tend to get repetitive at some points since some maps can get pretty big. The lighting could have been better since I barely noticed and ambient occlusion or shadows. The game also comes with some cool weather effects as well as the map texture and weather changing when winter comes which I thought was cool.

Sadly while the game runs at over 200+ fps there are hitches and stutters throughout the play session. Specifically, when you move around the camera the game just lags a bit for some reason and I've tried everything from v-sync on or off to g-sync without any success in solving the issue. There's also some huge fps drops or stutters when winter comes and the textures change. 

Graphics and tech analysis score: 7.5/10

[h1]The conclusion[/h1]
Northgard is a fine RTS game, one I recommend at any price mainly because its an indie title that can surpass even triple-A games and the gameplay and universe is something anyone can enjoy even if they're simplistic. With a better story campaign, some voice acting, more varied locations/zones and deeper mechanics this can easily become one of the best RTS games in the market. 

[h1]Final score: 7.5/10[/h1]

I played a lot of RTS games in the past, and have experienced firsthand many different skill levels and sources of joy from these games. But eventually, like most people, I gave up on them. There are multiple factors to explain why they have fallen out of favor, but to me the biggest of all is how input-demanding they all were if you really want to get good at them. As a kid you could simply play the campaign, build an immense army and then win the game all in one go. Against friends at that age, no one knew what they were doing so it was usually a simple but chaotic fun game. But nowadays everyone has access to basic strategies, and the players got much better. The amount of strategies possible in these kind of games are really cool but all of them require you to play really fast, having a lot of actions per minute (APM). It gets to the point it's actually stressful playing a match and I'd get tired from a short play session.
 
Northgard solves the problem I mentioned above and many others from this genre. It's a modern take on RTS games and many mechanics changed dramatically from classics, a lot of them for the best. By modern I mean not only innovative but also accessible, and it's orders of magnitude more accessible than any other game from the genre. The accessibility comes primarily from eliminating a lot of the required "micro" actions the player would have to manage in a regular RTS game. Note though that it [b]IS NOT[/b] in any way a dumbed down version of the regular gameplay loop, the engaging gameplay is still there but now you can actually take your time executing your strategy and if you really liked the micro then don't worry, some of it made through and still feel really meaningful while also not overwhelming the player. The simplest things like villagers being generated automatically changes so much how the game could be played and as soon as you try it you won't want to go back to the old way.

A few mechanics were added to compensate this change, and they were all really well thought out. Winter is one of them, and it affects two of your main resources and usually your military power. So 1/4 of the game is spent in this state with harsher conditions and it's something you have to actively think about and accomodate within your strategy. Another mechanic is making the environment hostile. You'll find plenty of creatures, hazards, neutral factions (that can become either allies or enemies depending on how you treat them) and even events. Events are some specific occurences that happens to all players and is announced ahead of time so the players can react and adjust to. These are overall great additions and it adds a layer unexplored in the genre, making you to deal with the environment as well as your opponent.

I want to go more in depth about adapting and there is a crucial mechanic that makes it work so well. The map is divided in tiles, and you'll gain territory by gaining control of these tiles one by one. Starting out the game you'll have only one tile, and no vision of what's around you. The darkened tiles are equivalent to the fog of war, and must be scouted before you can conquer them. In these tiles there will be multiple different resources that you need and even the tile itself could have some special effect. Resources location can be adjusted with map generation but are pretty fair by default while also not being the same every single time, so that the player has to adapt and play the cards they were dealt. One last thing about tiles is that they prevent the conventional "rushing" which was a big part of being forced to play fast in older RTS games.

Another thing this game explores much further with impressive results are alternate win conditions. It's not a new thing but here there are 4 default win conditions and could have a 5th depending on the map you're playing. Some of the clans will have a specialty but by no means they are forced to go for that specific win condition. The important takeaway is that they're all viable, and most clans can go for most of them under certain conditions. It's a cool element to consider and strategize, especially in team games.

This also brings me to the next topic: the clans and the variety among them. In the base game the clans are simple, but still pretty distinct from one another. The additional clans (which unfortunately are extra content you have to pay for, although they are not expensive and often go on sale along with the game) are really fun and introduce a lot of unique mechanics, making the game experience a lot more varied. Some of them turn base apsects of the game on its head and their strategies can vary wildly from more conventional clans. Another one of the things that differentiate one clan from another is the knowledge tree, one of the two talent trees in this game that are also great additions to make every match feel different. The other talent tree does not change but help accomodate different strategies, allowing for more ways to play the same clan.

Even in game modes this game can bring something new to the table. Conquest is a 2 player co-op campaign where every level has permanent buff during the campaign for each player and wildly different objectives and game rules. These are a lot harder than regular matches against AI because of the different obstacles and goals and also play pretty differently, making for a really fun experience where team play is essential.

To top it all off, the norse mythology theme is such a good choice as it ties itself with the mechanics and make for a very easy to present game, with familiar creatures and relics that also allows the team to have some creativity and create some different units with fun effects. The rest of the presentation also makes the effort to keep things simple but still very effective and it's very clear for example in the UI where a lot of useful information is available at a glance and simple tooltips complement them very well.

With all of these steps in the right direction, Northgard really is, in my opinion, a breath of fresh air and the future of RTS.

[h2] Northgard [/h2]

This is a quite engaging RTS, notable for the fact that victory through military might is not the main focus, but just one of the many ways to win. It essentially makes it like 4DX, but still a real-time strategy game with an emphasis on balanced development.

You will need to pay equal attention to food and resources, defense, happiness, and financial well-being, choosing a well-considered and correct development strategy while taking into account the characteristics of your clan.

The clans in the game are quite diverse. Although their buildings often differ only slightly (with paid clans being an exception), their playstyles vary significantly! The Raven clan excels in trade (there is a trade victory condition). The Deer clan is balanced and suitable for beginners. The Goat clan has plenty of food, while the Bear clan has an additional military unit (a bear, surprisingly), and so on.

Overall, the game is highly replayable, not demanding on hardware, and especially shines in PvP with other players. Therefore, for those who love strategy games and for some reason haven't tried it yet - I highly recommend it.

Like Age of Empires, but on a very intimate and small level. You take control of one of many clans to fight for dominance on the new continent of Northgard.
The map is split up into small areas that you can claim for yourself, given you have the resources for it. If you can't defend it however, someone else can, and will take it by force and claim it for themselves.
Your amount of units is around 10-20, less or more depending on time, going out to pillage and burn your opponents land.

The game requres a good amount of resource management, making every area you own count, and every area you loose problematic. Every nine months of summer are followed by three months of winter, where your resouce gathereing skills are put to the test. If you can't stay fed and warm during winter, it could spell your death. But so for the others as well. Taking away one of their precious sources of food just before winter is the most diabolic thing you can do.

Matches last between 30 minutes and an hour, usually, and are both challenging on a resource level, and a combat level.
Military engagements are usually fought on one front, but more experienced players can attack with two different forces, and while your enemy tries to fight off your main army, you can destroy one of their precious defense towers.

The game never has a dull moment, and every engagement has to be economically justified, making this a game less about who got the most units, but who can afford to feed them.

I’ve never reviewed a game before, but this is an absolute gem and I felt compelled.
Any bad observation about the game, is said with love – and in hope that this game will grow from the community’s feedback.

[h1]Overall feel[/h1]
Being an old-time fan of the genre, I’ve played many never games, hoping to get a bit of the magic that the classics had, such as Warcraft II, old C&C games etc. But most games fall short.
Nothgard achieves this splendidly, with a fresh take.

The game is well executed, in a unique blend of RTS paired with a sort of capture the flag mechanism.
In order to expand and build more, you need to take over a new area, and this works really well.

Resource management is key, and can be quite difficult, too difficult at times. But it extends the gameplay vastly. If it wasn’t such a key element, a skirmish game would be over too quickly.

[h1]Story mode[/h1]
The campaign mode is beautifully narrated with authentic accent and proper pronunciation of old Norse words. Being used to the pop-culturized pronunciations from both movies and games, this excellent voice acting was a positive surprise that adds a little special something to the game.

Unfortunately, the campaign is too short, took me about 10H to complete, including retries.
If I went through the campaign again, there would probably be 5-7H game time in it.

Adding more campaigns would greatly add value to the game.

[h1]Skirmish game[/h1]
Skirmish mode is excellent, each map is generated so you won’t see the same map twice. This adds a lot of value and replay-ability to it.

I’ve tried 3 different map types so far, but unfortunately couldn’t tell the difference.
If there is any, it might be a good idea to add map type information to the game configuration screen.

Certain areas have a boost to production, such as wood and lore. But there are also strategic areas, granting a damage boost to your troops and other perks. Controlling these areas can be key to victory. Only wish there were more unique areas and perks.

Each clan have unique benefits. Depending on the clan chosen, these benefits changes the gameplay a lot, adding additional fun and hours of gameplay.

Unfortunately you won’t ever see the heroes from the story mode again. Instead you get a Warchief, which doesn’t make sense to me at all. Why strip the characters you’ve built for each clan from the game?
It’s like getting a generic plumber instead of Mario.
Granting unique perks to each hero or warchief, instead of only the clan, would add additional depth to the gameplay.

[h1]Bugs[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Loading screen is blank, have to alt-tab to view it, even though it is the only open application
    [*]Lore generation continues after all “technologies” have been unlocked, triggering the notification that you can invest in a new technology even though there’s none left
    [*]Loading screen often crashes in campaign mode if progressing directly from one mission to the next
[/list]

[h1]Final thoughts[/h1]
Overall a great and well-polished game, but it would benefit greatly from more content.
More map variation, clans, units and buildings -especially unique.
Campaign difficulty could be polished a bit more, but that might just be me being sh***y at it

Would love to see a “colonization” game mode, where you start with building your home, and conquer new maps for trade and perks with the goal of eventually conquering the new world or something. Enemy could attack an area, forcing you to re-visit it to regain control or defend it.

Northgard is one of the tightest experiences I've ever played.

Everything works the same way - but differently.

Everyone is just your villagers, given different tasks - even your military units. So provided you have the cash, you can refit your warband to the task at hand.

The economy is all about flows, generated by said villagers. If you have a positive food flow, your stockpile will go up, and if it's negative, it'll go down. Same for gold, and wood. Villagers can learn to gather pretty much anything, and as soon as they're tasked, they start generating resources. Once again, all these systems work the same way, but with different tweaks.

Combat is small, and not overly focused on a clickfest to retask units and so on. I think the low population caps help with this. There are few enough unit types that you feel you can master them all, but enough to still provide a bit of variety. Like, if you're going up against towers, you know you need shieldbearers, that kind of thing. 

There's enough going on that you always feel like you're about to lose track, but not so much that it's inevitable. It's real seat-of-your-pants stuff, and for me at least, it pulls me into a flow state right from the start. The game, and its systems, just fit in to the human working memory, and the set-and-forget nature of a lot of the subsystems (the fact that villagers won't just stand around idle, for example) make it easy to grow your camp without having it grow beyond your ability to manage it.

I'd like some slightly more complex rally point mechanics, and some slightly smarter behaviour from villagers (why not have them start working in a building as soon as they finish it?) but overall this game is just beautifully crafted and seriously hits my sweet spot for RTS.

Ahoy! Northgard is a chilled-out Viking RTS with beautiful landscapes and soundtracks. The usual 4x elements are there, but with less of an emphasis on rush and perhaps more weight to pragmatic choices and balancing your economy. A standard match has you found your Clan, explore & tame the land, then aspire to either fame, riches, lore mastery or military conquest.

There are several game modes to play: Story, Conquest, Solo, Multiplayer - along with a second, optional DLC Story campaign, Cross of Vidar. To be honest, I never see any reason to play Solo or Multiplayer, although apparently the multiplayer scene is quite lively. The Story campaigns are "ok" but offer little replay value, since they are static scenarios you have to overcome. The real gem behind Northgard is the Conquest mode, something added several years after release and even surprised the Developers with how popular it was.

Conquest mode sees you take control of a clan and play a gauntlet of increasingly difficult, yet randomised, missions with randomised power-up rewards that you have to choose between. Each Conquest run feels unique thanks to the different clan mechanics and the way the power-ups interact with them. This may explain why Northgard decided to double-down on releasing Clan DLC, as it enriched both multiplayer and Conquest players. 

Speaking of Clan DLC, there really is a LOT of them, with more on the way. Whilst completely optional, they are reasonably priced (around $5 each) and better yet frequently on sale. To take each Clan through a Conquest will take 5-10 hours, longer if you are on a higher difficulty or learning a complicated clan such as Snake or Dragon. They all have unique mechanics and Hero units and (mostly) feel equally powerful. 

Northgard also has various cosmetic unlockables, such as Hero & building skins, all of which are earned in-game via story completion or spending achievement granted currency. It's a refreshing throwback to an era before publisher greed.

Thanks to it's Paradox-like DLC release schedule, Northgard still gets frequent free base-game updates six years after launch. The most recent one (at time of writing) has just revamped two biomes with gorgeous new textures and revamped diplomacy. I appreciate the care and time put into these updates.

Northgard takes a while to learn, but once you've reached the point where you can somewhat confidently build up a stable economy and sustain your population while commanding a handful of warriors, the frustration goes away (for the most part) and the game becomes incredibly fun. On higher difficulties it's pretty fast-paced, but you don't have to make good use of every single second. The game can actually be pretty relaxing, and the cute graphics and nice score greatly contribute to an overall pleasant experience during the hundreds of hours you will likely end up playing Northgard for.

Random negative events throughout the game, such as rat infestation or blizzard, add a welcome variety to the gameplay, and so do the various scenarios in the conquest mode with a wide range of objectives and special conditions and bonuses. In fact, the vast majority of my game time has been spent in co-op conquests with my fiancée, as I personally find it more engaging and varied than ranked multiplayer games. Kudos to Shiro for including this game mode! That being said, story mode is probably the best way for new players to gradually learn the game mechanics and try out different clans, while at the same time becoming a bit more immersed in the Viking world through a simple but enjoyable story.

There are by now more than a dozen clans you can play for, each offering a sufficiently different experience, giving the game pretty much an infinite replayability. Among my favorite clans are the simpler ones, e.g., Wolf, Boar, Stag, Ox and Horse, as opposed to those that require tedious micromanagement, e.g., Raven, Dragon or Rat (one exception for me is the clan of Lynx, which requires a certain amount of micromanagement, yet I still find it fun to play for). Anyway, with the current selection, you're guaranteed to sooner or later find one or more clans that suit your playstyle.

The only gripe I have with Northgard is the AI, which lacks any intelligence whatsoever and relies blatantly on cheating. On extreme difficulty, their cheating can be extremely frustrating – as you can see in the post-game stats, their resource income is several times higher than yours right from the beginning, which gives them virtually unlimited resources, which in turn allows them to sustain a large army at all times and prevents them from suffering during blizzards and other events. In a co-op conquest, you have to typically deal with six such opponents, often as a single team, which can be a total nightmare. At the same time, the AI enemies often just hang around with their armies or harass your edge territories and then withdraw, whereas if they wanted to, they could just make a push for your town hall and decimate you in a matter of minutes with those armies of theirs. Nevertheless, at the second highest difficulty level, the game feels boring at times.

So, while I greatly appreciate the amazing job Shiro has been doing balancing the game mechanics over the years, regularly adding new content and now even planning to extend the story mode, I think investing time into substantially improving the AI would be in order.

Northgard is one of those games that you like immediately in the menu. When the game loads up, it feels crisp, clean, intuitive, and runs like a gem. Some people have mentioned stability issues, but I guess I was just lucky because it ran smooth throughout for me; just a second or so freeze when Winter starts and goes.

People seem to like reviews that are pros and cons/suggestions related, so here we go.

Pros:
- Butter smooth, awesome visuals. 
- Combines Survival with RTS, you really need to keep an eye on your resources, a bad winter really messes with your tribe- love that!
- Not purely warfare based; you pick your clan, each with their own playstyle, and though you can have warriors and chieftains in every clan, you can win by playing it your way, bringing us to the next one:
- Multiple victory conditions, from establishing trade routes to warfare, or conquering Yggdrasil, there are multiple ways to stay in the game, I honestly can not WAIT for Multiplayer

Cons / Suggestions - baring in mind it's Early Access
- Fairly limited at this point; 2 hours into play, 1 hour to learn and 1 hour to play a full game from start to finish with medium AI (3 of them) and I won my first try as Trader, and I really, really didn't do it very well. Looking back I made all sorts of horrible decisions. 
- Map size; [b]in my opinion[/b] discovering other factions happens way too fast, and once you do, you're basically out of room for improvement. This may be by design, to force interaction between players earlier on, but in AI mode it feels a bit stuffy- this may be the way the devs have playtested it and it maybe feels right in multiplayer to force interaction with each other
- Early Access. Typical of early access titles, this one just over all feels like it needs "more" - but that's precisely the point for releasing it now, it gets rid of bugs and optimizes performance, as well as getting some much desired feedback for the devs. 

Overall:

This game is the first Early Access title that I personally find extremely promising; the reason for that is simple: this is the first Early Access game that I will continue playing, since it is [b]already[/b] a proper functioning, well fleshed out game, that simply needs a bit 'more', to keep us hooked. This is a solid gaming investment.

Keep up the good work devs!

Northgard follows our clan of Norse based Vikings as we explore the hostile lands around us, complete with myth and legend in the form of draugr, wyverns, kobolds, giants and more.

[h1]Humble Norse Beginnings[/h1]

Like most strategy games, we start with humble beginnings. Our clan – of which you can choose from six (plus 2 additional DLC clans), each with their own unique abilities, strengths and weaknesses to suit different playstyles – has nothing but a few villagers and a headquarters. We must start by placing a few simple buildings, such as a scout to check the surrounding territory, a woodcutter to start harvesting wood so that we can expand, and a house, to allow our village to grow. Villagers who don’t have a unique job will automatically collect food from the surrounding area where possible, whilst others will have a specialist workplace.

As the scouts check out nearby territory we will find land that is suitable for different purposes. For example, some land contains a farmland, fish in a lake or deer that can be hunted. In these territories we’d want to build the appropriate food building, along with a granary, to make sure the rats don’t get at our food supplies, which can also spread sickness, which has a knock on effect to your clan happiness and growth. Happiness needs to be balanced as your villagers will have certain expectations of you as their leader. Don’t worry though, you can always bribe them with booze! In other tiles you’ll find other events, such as ruins to explore, neutral clans to trade with or even special unique goals that can even win the game, such as capturing Yggdrasil, the world tree. Some territories are defended by neutral monsters or factions and you’ll need to develop an army to overcome them.

[h1]Winter Approaches[/h1]

The game has a month-year cycle which affects gameplay and again, requires forward thinking. As spring passes into summer onto autumn and winter looms ahead, you’ll need to be stockpiling food and wood for your fires. Starvation and cold can stifle growth and slowly kill through sickness and disease, although this isn’t quite the same level as Frostpunk. You also have other penalties in the winter, such as reduced army strength – so pick those battles well! Spring will always come back around, so it’s matter of resource management, time and patience.

As you expand, it becomes more and more expensive to colonize more land. This means you have to think ahead and choose wisely, because the order in which you spread out over the land and build can be critical to gameplay. This is an extremely slow paced small scale strategy game; there’s no crazy hotkey play like Starcraft II here and it doesn’t have large army management such as in Age of Empires. Instead, this is something new – a hybrid real time strategy that reminds me more of the 4X and Civilization series than what you might usually expect from an RTS.

[h1]This is a slow-paced chilled out strategy[/h1]

As such, this might be too slow paced for some and it does fall into the trap of occasionally being so slow paced that you’re simply sitting around, waiting for stuff to happen. No one wants empty downtime in a game, but this is quite common at the very beginning whilst you’re building up your mini-empire. It’s a shame, that there’s a risk that people will be put off by this, and not explore the full scope of the game – as it really opens up later on when there’s a lot more management and important decisions to be made.

[h1]Single Player or PvP[/h1]

Northgard’s single player campaign has a simple storyline of vengeance and betrayal. It’s quite mundane, predictable and doesn’t have very strong writing, but it does give extensive tutorials and helps progress through all of the clans and environments you’ll have at your disposal in PvP. It’s a good learning tool, but you might find it a little boring towards the end. I personally enjoyed it, but some maps were a little too long and there was too much waiting around. It took me around 20 hours to complete the campaign, with its 11 maps, each with bonus (hard mode) win conditions.

Most of the meat of the game will come from PvP, but this has it’s own problems in that any PvP game relies on the community. Northgard is a fairly niche strategy game, that loans itself more towards chilling out slowly than fighting fiercely. In a long game, with a small community, you’ve got a reasonable chance that your opponents might leave (especially when most games will take at least an hour or more), which is frustrating. Waits for matches can also be quite long. It’s definitely still worth delving into PvP, and the flaws here are present in most PvP games with small communities so most will be familiar with them. 

To add replayability and add more competition to the game, there’s an overall PvP leaderboard, as well as seasonal rankings. I’m not sure this game will ever be an eSport, as it’s far too slow to maintain high viewer retention or excitement, but this does add a competitive motivation for those who are so inclined. On a more casual level, if you have friends who play then the PvP could be absolutely amazing and extremely fun with lots of depth and thought required.

[h1]The Future?[/h1]

Since release, Shiro Games have continued to support Northgard, with both premium DLC (two bonus clans that are entirely optional but do add new strategies and gameplay) and with a large free update called Ragnarok, which brought a new map, new tiles and special events. At the time of writing, a free update called the Winter Festival is ongoing, which brings new elements such as frozen waters, as well as cute snowmen that your villages will build! Development is on-going, with promises of lots of new content to come in the future, which I’m really looking forward to.

[h1]Final Thoughts, aka TL:DR[/h1]

In conclusion, Northgard is a unique strategy game, one which won’t appeal to everyone, but for those who are looking for a relaxed RTS experience that has depth and many ways to play out, this ticks all the boxes.

Quirky, addictive, challenging, rewarding ... I thought that this game might be fun, yet I was positively surprised.

First off, don't let the graphics fool you. It's not an easy game. The level of (micro and other) management you have to deal with is demanding. There's always something you don't have enough of: food, wood, money, happiness, .population, ... and then the winter months hit you, putting a strain on both food and wood ... it's a balancing act to grow your realm. It's not as easy as building a large army, because every fighter isn't producing something your settlement needs, yet still needs to maintained because they need to eat. But sooner or later you'll have improve your buildings and works to the point where everything just clicks. Speaking of which ...

There's always something to improve. Get new territory by clearing a region with your fighters (and integrate it into your realm by (usually) paying food), mine stone and iron to improve your buildings (so that they'll produce more and accept more workers) and jobs and fighters, build a relict that enhances a single aspect of your realm or grants you a special ability, win combats to choose one of three unit upgrade trees, acquire lore (mostly by working special "buildings" like stone circles you find in the wilderness) to get improvements from the tech tree, and more.

The victory conditiions are varied and interesting. And there's always something to do. A campaign, daily and weekly tasks, and (the best part for me) Conquests. There's a bunch of different clans in the base game, and each one has their own Conquests (a series of matches with pre-determined victory conditions, and each match grants you a new ability for your clan during all Conquests).

When I bought the game I never imagined to get the different DLC clans. There's already plenty in the base game, would I really want to shell out more cash just to get a new clan with slightly different rules? Turns out that yes, I do, because every new clan also comes with their own set of Conquests.

If you like the idea of a RTS with an emphasis on challenging base building, this game is for you. But beware: if this is indeed your cup of tea, it might be seriously addictive.

Northgard captured the feeling I had playing Warcraft II and Warcraft III when they were new. It is not mechanically like either of these games; but the quality of the game experience itself is the same.

What makes Northgard so wonderful in the RTS genre is the economic and environmental layers it adds. You are not merely building armies to fight other armies; you are trying to survive the winter, keep people happy, and stay out of debt. You don't just win by killing everyone else, you can economically dominate your opponents, become the most famous clan, or discover the most lore. Some maps even bring their own unique victory conditions. There's a mix of aggressive and defensive playstyles for everyone, though it's important to remember that you are vikings; you can't be too passive or you will lose.

Northgard is a great case study in what good game design looks like. The player is given several easy to understand interdependent systems to manage and then is thrown into an environment that forces you to adapt your strategy to what you have available. Games feel shorter than they are because all of these systems are engaging and keep you struggling against time as the yearly in-game cycle keeps you adapting and reacting to the changing conditions while enemies expand, monsters and wildlife attack, events trigger, and objectives trade hands.

This is a fantastic game; an absolute gem. I recommend it to anyone with any interest in RTS, 4X, grand strategy, or simulation games - as this game borrows ideas from across the spectrum and uses them to create a really well thought out and always engaging to play experience.

Northgard is a very chill, easy-to-learn RTS with a surprising amount of depth.

This is not a game about playing faster than your opponent or having god-tier micro. Micro can give you options and a small edge, but the real game is economy and tempo management. Most matches feel closer to PvE than PvP: you’re expanding, securing territory, and ramping up resource production while trying not to fall behind the global pace of the game.

You’re not really fighting your opponents directly — you’re fighting the phase of the game itself. Fall behind in tempo and you die.

The design works best in FFA or team games. In FFA, recovery is sometimes possible because players naturally gang up on whoever is ahead. In team vs team, the goal is usually to snowball as hard as possible before an inevitable decisive battle decides the match.

Think less “high-APM unit control” and more “strategically staying on the power curve.” Success is about keeping up with the average progression and not slipping.

That said, the game is extremely punishing. Major combat losses or failing to survive winter can end your game outright. Population growth is a constant bottleneck, so you can’t easily recover from decisive defeats. One bad mistake can be terminal.

Overall, it’s a very niche RTS.

It also has a campaign (fine, but not a selling point) and large randomized challenge trials, which are a big selling point if you’re into single-player or 2-player co-op content.

I have a lot of fun, over 200+ hours now of just doing solo and co-op conquest with friends-- I still haven't even finished all the clans in conquest yet. A friend and I got this many years ago to play as a non-standard kind of RTS. In some ways the game was great fun and in others very frustrating. As the game picked up years and new DLC were released, issues with connectivity were not fixed, balance issues around new clans were constant, and the core mechanic around the game stayed the same, i.e. you need to econ or you will fail.

You could call this game an RTS, but that would be mistaking how slow this game can be and how clans can go without focusing on troops at all. Games can take hours and that only makes the connectivity issues worse when you are trying to play any multiplayer.

I don't dislike the game, but it seems to be lacking the love it needs to not be chore to play at times. A frustrating game stops being enjoyable, which is why my friend and I have stopped playing and why I would not recommend this game to others.

Anyone complaining about the amount of DLC needs to take a step back and get some perspective.

The game has been out for 7 years and has received consistent free updates and added factions. Some DLC are better than others, ones that are poorly received are typically re-worked and improved. Each faction DLC introduces a faction that typically significantly changes the way you play the game, creating huge replayability regardless if you're more interested in single player, co-op or multiplayer. People comparing it to the Sims need to settle down; sales happen often and you can currently (hippogriff clan release sale) purchase the game and all available content for sub $60. 

Numerous game modes, procedural map generations and consistent free content updates keep the game feeling fresh and interesting even 7 years on. No microtransactions. Cosmetics you can unlock with gameplay. This is honestly one of the best values in gaming, and I strongly recommend it to anyone who likes rts/4x games or city builder sims.

Despite being an RTS, Northgard plays more like a Civ game, in which your primary focus is maintaining balance between happiness, food, wood, lore (science), krowns (money), and military power. Since each map is randomly generated, you'll find that your approach to victory depends not only on your chosen faction but also the resources available near your starting position. This map generation is what keeps this game replayable and repeatable.

However I must admit that combat can be repetitive, since at the moment there are only three types of fighting units. Some factions have unique warchiefs (general unit) but their attack power is more or less the same. Their uniqueness affects resource management instead.

CONS
- Right now, there are no hotkeys yet for units, which make defending and microing against attacks a chore.
- Repetitive combat, needs more unit types, with more unique mechanics.
- Needs customizable victory conditions. Whenever you start a game, you can tick boxes if you want a fame victory, trade victory, domination victory, etc. But the magnitude of these victory conditions are fixed. For example, fame victory requires 1200 fame---I wish there was a slider that allows me to change this to mayble 1400 or 1000 fame. I really think these victory sliders would allow players to decide how long each game lasts, since each game lasts roughly about an hour.

PROS
+Randomly generated maps, map objectives and map events make each playthrough challenging and unique.
+System requirements are quite low. The game can run on low end PC's and laptops
+Decent comeback mechanics. Being beaten in a fight does not mean you lose the game.
+Easy to learn, hard to master. 

DEPENDS ON TASTE
+/- Economy management requires IQ. Not only do you have to sustain your town's needs in a summer/winter cycle, you also have to prepare for game events. Thankfully these events have early warnings (usually several months ahead of such catastrophe) so if you mess up, it's probably your own fault for mismanaging your resources. I like this challenge, though I know of others who hate it.

I recommend this game, especially if you like Civ and would like to play a more casual, RTS version of it

Northgard is one part RTS and one part city building. I'd describe it as Banished meets Age of Empires.

You build buildings that allow you to specialize your population (There's a building for warriors, woodcutters, miners etc) but you can only build so many buildings per area of the map you control (usually 3-5. each area can be upgraded 1 time to allow an extra building). Because of this it's very important to properly time your colonization so you don't end up gimping your clan by running out of space to put new houses or resource collection to offset the growing population. 

The victory types are fairly broad and support a variety of playstyles.

Wisdom: Unlock 4 blessings of the Gods in the Lore Tree and have at least 4 loremasters working.
Domination: Destroy the Town Hall of all the other players. 
Fame: Control 12 areas, obtain 1000 fame and build the Altar of Kings.
Trade: collect 9000 krowns, have 1000 in stock and four active merchants/sailors.
Map Special: Can be turned off but each of the 3 maps has a unique victory you can aim for. 

Pros: 

Very easy to learn
AI difficulty scales well
Great immersion from the soundtrack and graphics
Active Developers (bought the game during initial release and they have since added 3 more clans, 6 total, and continued to update balance, a campaign is also in progress). 

Cons:

Somewhat lacking in strategy
limited replay value
Would be nice to have a special map that can host all 6 clans at once (max 4 per game currently) 

Tldr; Overall I'd give it a solid 8/10. With a few updates to give some more strategic choice/depth and an option to choose what map you play + make the map bigger it'd be a great casual RTS experience for you and a few friends to see who will rule Northgard. I've bought a lot of abandoned Early Access games over the years so the eagerness of the developers is a good sign for me. Not overpriced at full price but definitely worth picking up on a sale.
